items.t: Saudi Arabian Fertilizer stock gets Bangladesh export boost
sum: Saudi Arabian Fertilizer stock gains a fresh export-demand signal after Bangladesh approved urea imports from SABIC Agri-Nutrients on Thursday, November 12, 2026. The decision covers two lots for the country's 2026-27 fertilizer program, according to The Business Standard.

The Cabinet Committee on Government Purchase approved the import of 295,000 metric tonnes of fertilizer from Morocco, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, alongside purchases from a local producer. The package includes granular urea, triple superphosphate and diammonium phosphate.

SABIC Agri-Nutrients will provide 80,000 tonnes of bulk granular urea in two 40,000-tonne lots. The first lot carries a price of 432.50 US dollars per tonne, while the second is priced at 430.83 US dollars per tonne.

For investors, the approval points to an additional sales channel for the Saudi fertilizer producer. It does not, by itself, determine the company's profitability: realized urea prices, freight expenses and plant utilization will continue to shape margins as the deliveries proceed.

The two SABIC Agri-Nutrients lots form part of Bangladesh's planned fertilizer procurement for the 2026-27 fiscal year. The committee also approved urea imports from Fertiglobe Distributions and purchases from Bangladesh's Karnaphuli Fertiliser Company.

Saudi fertilizer shares remain linked to global crop-nutrient demand and the ability of producers to move product into export markets. Investors will therefore focus on shipment execution and the contribution of new orders to sales volumes.
Broader fertilizer-market developments can be followed in the Current market reports.

items.t: SABIC stock: Fujian complex on track for Q4 2026 startup
sum: SABIC's Fujian petrochemical complex remains on track to start operations in the fourth quarter of 2026 after three plants completed trial runs, Arab News reported on October 26. Chief Executive Faisal Al-Faqeer said the plants, which mainly produce polyethylene and polypropylene, completed the trials on their first attempt.

The update adds an execution milestone to SABIC's selective-growth strategy in China and Asia. The company reported adjusted third-quarter net income of 224.3 million US dollars, recovering from an adjusted loss of 101.4 million US dollars in the second quarter. Revenue rose 14 percent quarter on quarter to 7.52 billion US dollars, while adjusted EBITDA increased 40 percent to 1.26 billion US dollars, according to Arab News.

SABIC said its transformation program had generated 950 million US dollars of recurring EBITDA improvement year to date, against a target of 3 billion US dollars by 2030. Management said the gains come from structural cost reductions, production reliability and commercial performance.

The company also lowered its 2026 capital expenditure guidance to 3.3 billion US dollars, citing capital efficiency and project prioritization. Separately, SABIC Agri-Nutrients approved a new Jubail facility expected to produce 2.6 million tonnes of urea and 1.2 million tonnes of ammonia annually, with commercial operations planned for the fourth quarter of 2030.
SABIC stock traded at 48.50 Saudi riyals on Tadawul at 3:17 p.m. Riyadh time on Wednesday, November 11, 2026.

SABIC is headquartered in Riyadh and operates across Chemicals, Polymers and Agri-Nutrients. The company serves customers in more than 140 countries across the Americas, Europe, the Middle East and Africa, and Asia Pacific. SABIC describes itself as one of the top three largest global chemical companies. Its diversified portfolio and geographic reach distinguish it from more specialized chemical producers, although its earnings remain exposed to industry cycles, feedstock costs and logistics.
Saudi equities remain part of the broader regional market environment; see Current market reports.

Saudi Arabian Fertilizer stock faces logistics squeeze before rebound
sum: Saudi Arabian Fertilizer stock is exposed to a difficult near-term operating environment for Gulf fertilizer producers. An AGBI analysis by Matt Smith, published on October 8, said disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz had restricted exports and pushed transport costs sharply higher.

According to the analysis, logistics costs for fertilizer shipped through alternative routes had risen above 200 US dollars per tonne, compared with about 50 US dollars before the conflict. Urea prices averaged about 420 US dollars per tonne in the third quarter, while production costs were estimated at 150 to 200 US dollars per tonne.

That combination leaves less room for profit after freight and has encouraged producers to be more selective with orders. SABIC Agri-Nutrients, Fertiglobe and Industries Qatar recorded first-half sales volumes below production capacity as transport economics deteriorated.

The pressure is not limited to one company, but it matters for SABIC Agri-Nutrients because the business relies on urea exports. AGBI cited analysts who expect global urea demand to exceed new supply over the next five years. Fertiglobe forecasts that additional demand will exceed additional supply by 2.3 million tonnes between 2026 and 2030.

For SABIC Agri-Nutrients, the longer-term backdrop contrasts with weaker recent earnings. The company’s first-half net profit fell 21 percent to 428 million US dollars, according to the analysis. A recovery therefore depends on both fertilizer pricing and a normalization of regional shipping routes.

Investors should treat the sector as a longer-term exposure rather than a short-term trading theme. The potential benefit of tighter supply remains conditional on freight costs, export access and the timing of a broader market recovery.
Saudi fertilizer shares remain exposed to the regional market backdrop; see Current market reports.

items.t: SABIC stock: adjusted Q3 earnings return to profit
sum: SABIC returned to positive adjusted earnings in the third quarter of 2026, according to the company's Q3 results announcement published on October 25. Adjusted net income reached SAR 0.84 billion, compared with an adjusted net loss of SAR 0.38 billion in the second quarter.

Revenue increased 14 percent quarter-on-quarter to SAR 28.17 billion. Adjusted EBITDA rose 40 percent to SAR 4.75 billion, while adjusted EBIT climbed 434 percent to SAR 2.17 billion. Adjusted earnings per share improved to SAR 0.28 from a loss of SAR 0.13 in the previous quarter.

The figures point to a sharp sequential improvement in profitability, although SABIC said geopolitical developments and market headwinds remained part of the operating environment. The company presented the quarterly recovery alongside a longer-term focus on portfolio optimization, transformation and selective growth.

SABIC said it had achieved SAR 3.56 billion, equivalent to USD 0.95 billion, of the positive recurring EBITDA impact targeted under its 2030 transformation program. The company also completed the divestment of its engineering thermoplastics business in the Americas and Europe for an enterprise value of USD 450 million.

Net debt stood at SAR 3.03 billion on September 30, compared with SAR 2.73 billion on June 30. SABIC also highlighted a final investment decision for a new ammonia and urea complex in Saudi Arabia and feedstock allocation for a new methanol plant in Jubail.

Headquartered in Riyadh, SABIC operates across the chemicals value chain through its Chemicals, Polymers and Agri-Nutrients strategic business units. The company serves customers in more than 140 countries across the Americas, Europe, the Middle East and Africa, and Asia Pacific. SABIC describes itself as one of the three largest global chemical companies, with a diversified international footprint rather than a single regional market focus.
Saudi market developments can be followed in current market reports.

Saudi Arabian Fertilizer reports 62.49 percent drop. Saudi Arabian Fertilizer stock gets 12 ratings
sum: Saudi Arabian Fertilizer (ISIN SA0007879139), now SABIC Agri-Nutrients Company, reported third-quarter net income of SAR 483.82 million, down from SAR 1,289.87 million a year earlier. MarketScreener reported the figures for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, on October 20, 2026.

The result reflects a sharper earnings decline than the revenue trend. Sales fell to SAR 3,219.51 million from SAR 3,521.53 million in the third quarter of 2025, while basic earnings per share from continuing operations decreased to SAR 1.02 from SAR 2.71.

finanzen.at said the revenue result exceeded the SAR 2.36 billion analyst estimate, while earnings per share came below the SAR 1.13 estimate. That contrast puts profitability ahead of sales growth as the immediate issue for investors.

The company is also tied to a major capacity project. SABIC said on October 25, 2026, that SABIC Agri-Nutrients had taken the final investment decision for an industrial complex with annual capacity of 1.20 million metric tons of ammonia and 2.60 million metric tons of urea. The urea capacity is planned to rise 54.00 percent from current levels.

The expansion gives the earnings story a longer-term counterweight, but its scale does not erase the third-quarter decline. The company operates across agricultural nutrients including urea, ammonia and phosphate products.

Market data show a market capitalization of SAR 53.1 billion and a 52-week range of SAR 107.00 to SAR 159.30 as of October 26, 2026. The current quotation is therefore in the lower part of that range, while the recent results provide the clearest dated operating test for the stock.

On the Saudi exchange, Saudi Arabian Fertilizer stock was last at SAR 111.60 on October 26, 2026 at 10:51 a.m. AST. The company remains positioned between near-term earnings pressure and a capacity expansion that could strengthen its production base over time.

SABIC Q3 2026 Results: Revenue Up 14%, Adjusted EBITDA Up 40% - News and Statistics
sum: SABIC Reports 14% Revenue Growth and 40% Rise in Adjusted EBITDA for Q3 2026

Saudi Basic Industries Corporation (SABIC) posted a 14 per cent quarter-on-quarter gain in revenue and a 40 per cent increase in adjusted EBITDA for the third quarter of 2026, according to its financial results. Revenue came in at SAR28.17 billion ($7.51 billion), while adjusted EBITDA climbed to SAR4.75 billion ($1.27 billion).

Adjusted EBIT jumped 434 per cent quarter-on-quarter to SAR2.17 billion ($580 million). Adjusted net income was SAR840 million ($220 million), swinging from an adjusted net loss of SAR380 million ($100 million) in the prior quarter. Adjusted earnings per share came to SAR0.28 ($0.07), compared with a loss of SAR0.13 ($0.03) per share in the second quarter.
As of September 30, 2026, net debt was SAR3.03 billion ($810 million), versus SAR2.73 billion ($730 million) at the end of June.

Dr Faisal Alfaqeer, CEO and Executive Member of the Board, said the quarter showed exceptional resilience amid geopolitical developments and market headwinds, supported by a clear forward-looking vision and continued focus on strategic objectives including portfolio optimisation, transformation and selective growth, aimed at long-term profitability and shareholder value creation.

Among key developments in the quarter, SABIC Agri-Nutrients took a final investment decision to build a new ammonia and urea complex in Saudi Arabia, with yearly capacities of 1.2 million tonnes of ammonia and 2.6 million tonnes of urea. The project is expected to lift the company's urea production capacity by 54 per cent over current levels.
The Ministry of Energy also assigned feedstock for a new methanol plant in Jubail with an annual capacity of 1.8 million tonnes, supporting SABIC's expansion in strategic markets.

sum: Saudi Basic Industries Corporation (SABIC, ISIN SA0007879121) received an A+ long-term rating with a stable outlook after Fitch affirmed the assessment on October 20, 2026, as Argaam reported. SABIC also scheduled its third-quarter 2026 results discussion for October 26, 2026, according to Argaam.

On October 9, 2026, SABIC Agri-Nutrients approved an ammonia and urea complex that would raise annual urea capacity from 4.8 million to 7.4 million metric tons, a project detail carried by MarketScreener.
On October 20, 2026, Fitch affirmed the A+ rating and stable outlook; its report also said SABIC shipments fell 33 percent quarter over quarter in the second quarter of 2026, according to Argaam.

Also on October 20, 2026, SABIC set October 26, 2026 for its third-quarter results discussion, while the published consensus cited by Argaam called for net profit of SAR 86.26 million versus SAR 435.5 million a year earlier.

Fitch's assessment gives investors a quantified view of SABIC's financial cushion. The agency cited cash and short-term investments of SAR 40 billion at the end of June 2026 against current debt of SAR 3.2 billion, while expecting 2026 capital spending of SAR 10 billion. SABIC's investor-relations page describes a business spanning chemicals, polymers, and agri-nutrients across more than 140 countries through three strategic business units.

The next company event is the third-quarter 2026 results discussion on October 26, 2026. SABIC's market capitalization stood at SAR 132.3 billion on October 21, 2026, while its 52-week range was SAR 43.76 to SAR 62.50.

SABIC stock was last at SAR 44.10 on Tadawul on October 21, 2026 at 12:17 p.m. AST. The investor-relations page presents SABIC as a global chemicals group with operations across the Americas, Europe, the Middle East and Africa, and Asia Pacific.

Saudi stocks plunge to lowest close since April 2021
sum: RIYADH —Saudi Arabia’s benchmark Tadawul All Share Index (TASI) closed Tuesday’s session down 1.7 percent, shedding 172 points to settle at 9,952 points. This marked its lowest closing level since April 2021, with total trading turnover reaching approximately SR3.8 billion.

During the session, the index fluctuated between a low of 9,941 points and a high of 10,116 points. Its losses since the beginning of the year have reached approximately 540 points, equivalent to a decline of 5.1 percent.

Several leading stocks came under selling pressure. Saudi Aramco shares fell one percent to SR25.48, while Al Rajhi Bank shares declined by a similar margin to SR60.15. Shares of Etihad Etisalat, BSF, and Al Yamamah Cement dropped between one percent and 3 percent, while Yanbu National Petrochemical Company (Yansab) plunged 7 percent.

Shares of SABIC Agri-Nutrients and Bank Albilad each declined by 3 percent, closing at SR109.80 and SR21.47, respectively, following the release of their Q3 2026 financial results. Tihama was the top decliner, tumbling 8 percent while Azm topped the gainers with a 4 percent increase.

items.t: Alphabet stock drops 12% and analysts eye $400
sum: Alphabet entered the final days of the first quarter in an uncomfortable position. Shares of the Google parent have fallen more than 12% year to date, trading near $274, and the stock has spent weeks below its key short- and medium-term moving averages. The pressure has come from multiple directions at once, and the most recent hit arrived from a Los Angeles courtroom.

On March 26, a Los Angeles jury found that Alphabet’s YouTube and Meta Platforms were negligent in protecting children on their platforms and had deliberately structured those platforms to maximize addictive behavior. The combined damages awarded totaled $6 million, a figure that by itself poses no financial threat to either company. The concern is what comes next.

Alphabet fell roughly 3% on the day of the verdict, a smaller drop than the nearly 8% decline suffered by Meta but significant enough to extend Alphabet’s slide toward bear market territory. The company has said it plans to appeal the ruling, with a spokesperson arguing that YouTube is a streaming platform rather than a social media site. That distinction may matter legally but did little to calm investors.

The risk is not the $6 million. It is the template the ruling creates. Teen social media addiction has become a legislative priority in several countries. Australia became the first nation to ban children under 16 from using social media platforms. European countries are at various stages of similar restrictions, and several Asian markets including Indonesia, Malaysia and the Indian state of Karnataka have implemented or are planning comparable bans. For Alphabet, YouTube accounts for less than 15% of total revenue, which limits its direct exposure compared with Meta. The ruling could also open new avenues for lawsuits targeting AI chatbots, which would affect a much broader range of technology companies.

Despite the turbulence, Wall Street has maintained a broadly constructive view of Alphabet’s longer-term prospects. Wells Fargo raised its price target on the stock from $387 to $397 on March 27, maintaining an overweight rating. The firm pointed specifically to Alphabet’s Tensor Processing Unit licensing program and its acquisition of cloud security company Wiz as potential revenue drivers.

items.t: Sabic posts biggest loss since 2003 amid asset sales and sector glut
sum: Sabic reported its largest annual loss in 22 years for 2025, taking an SAR 25.78 bn hit — surpassing Bloomberg analysts’ expectations of SAR 22.48 bn. Revenue slipped 1% y-o-y to SAR 116.53 bn, the company said in an earnings release (pdf).

The massive bottom-line loss is largely a deliberate accounting reset rather than an operational collapse. The company recorded SAR 15.2 bn in noncash losses from revaluing assets it is exiting in Europe and the Americas, alongside SAR 3.8 bn in provisions and impairments linked to a UK cracking unit.
REMEMBER- Sabic is slimming down its business, having agreed to sell its Europeanpetrochemicals and engineering thermoplastics units in an SAR 3.6 bn (USD 950 mn) divestment.

The company is still grinding through a brutal downcycle. “The decline in sales revenues was attributed to a decline in the average selling prices for the company products that came despite an increase in the sales volume,” Al Awwal Capital Equity Research Consultant Hesham El Shebeini tells EnterpriseAM. The primary culprit is a flood of new production capacity in China that has depressed global utilization rates and curbed income margins. High interest rates and low oil prices further squeezed worldwide demand, El Shebeini added.

Sabic is taking the pain now to structurally improve its bottom line for the future. Dumping legacy European and American operations shields Sabic from regions plagued by structural energy shortages and strict carbon emission rules.

A change in leadership: Abdulrahman Al Fageeh is stepping down as CEO to be replaced on 1 April by Faisal Al Faqeer (LinkedIn), an Aramco veteran with extensive experience in the refining and petrochemicals sectors.

The worst may be over for the Saudi petrochemical giant. Sabic is set to capture a major domestic feedstock advantage under Al Faqeer. “Jafurah gas project, which commenced operations recently, will increase Saudi daily production of ethane to 1.5 bcf/d, hence benefiting the Saudi petrochemicals industry,” El Shebeini points out. Combined with expected interest rate cuts and the exit of European competitors, the newly slimmed-down portfolio looks poised for a rebound.

Exclusive: SABIC tells Maaal divestment of European petrochemical assets and ETP averted $4 bln in future losses
sum: Saudi Basic Industries Corporation said it has taken strategic decisions to divest a number of assets outside Saudi Arabia, marking a significant shift in the management of its business portfolio, the company told Maaal.

The divestments, which included European petrochemical assets and ETP operations in the Americas and Europe, helped avert around $4 billion in potential future losses, SABIC said. The asset sales also spared the company up to $5 billion in shutdown and closure-related costs.

SABIC said the move was aimed at halting prolonged financial drain, improving capital allocation efficiency, and redirecting investments toward businesses with stronger profitability and more sustainable long-term prospects.

Salah bin Mohammed Al-Hareky, executive vice president of corporate finance at Saudi Basic Industries Corporation, told Maaal that the transactions are expected to halt losses of between $3.4 billion and $3.7 billion over the 2022–2025 period.
He added that the divestments would also avoid an additional $4 billion in anticipated future losses that would have continued had the assets remained in the company’s portfolio.

Salah bin Mohammed Al-Hareky said the losses were driven by structural shifts in global petrochemical markets, including substantial excess production capacity, intensifying competition from China, and environmental regulations that have increased costs, particularly in Europe.

He added that the global petrochemicals sector is facing prolonged pressure amid persistent oversupply and slowing demand growth. The situation has been especially pronounced in Europe, where weaker demand has pushed profit margins to their lowest levels in a decade.
